coverage: Complete dialogue in both English editions: two speakers, Lysias, named human/divine references, imaginary speech roles and chariot figures; context-scoped Hera and Zeno aliases.

entities.name: Socrates
entities.body: The Athenian philosopher discussing love, the soul and rhetoric with Phaedrus.

entities.name: Phaedrus
entities.body: Socrates’ companion, an admirer of Lysias with a passion for speeches.

entities.name: Lysias
entities.body: The Athenian speechwriter whose speech on love Phaedrus brings to the discussion.

entities.name: Cephalus
entities.body: Lysias and Polemarchus’s father.

entities.name: Acumenus
entities.body: The physician who is a friend of Socrates and Phaedrus, and Eryximachus’s father.

entities.name: Epicrates
entities.body: The Athenian hosting Lysias in the house associated with Morychus.

entities.name: Morychus
entities.body: The Athenian whose house is mentioned as the place where Lysias is staying.

entities.name: Pindar
entities.body: The Greek lyric poet quoted by Socrates.

entities.name: Herodicus
entities.body: The physician known for prescribing exercise, recalled for his walking regimen.

entities.name: Sappho
entities.body: The Greek lyric poet whom Socrates invokes as a source of inspiration about love.

entities.name: Anacreon
entities.body: The Greek lyric poet associated with love and song.

entities.name: Simmias of Thebes
entities.body: The friend of Socrates recalled as an unusually eager lover of argument.

entities.name: Ibycus
entities.body: The Greek lyric poet whom Socrates quotes.

entities.name: Homer
entities.body: The ancient Greek epic poet repeatedly cited in the conversation.

entities.name: Stesichorus
entities.body: The Greek lyric poet whose recantation about Helen inspires Socrates’ second speech.

entities.name: Pythocles
entities.body: Phaedrus’s father, playfully rendered as Vain Man in this translation.

entities.name: Euphemus
entities.body: Stesichorus’s father, rendered as Godly Man in the wordplay.

entities.name: Polemarchus
entities.body: Lysias’s brother, whom Socrates presents as interested in philosophy.

entities.name: Lycurgus
entities.body: The traditional Spartan lawgiver named in the discussion of enduring laws.

entities.name: Solon
entities.body: The Athenian lawgiver and poet.

entities.name: Darius I
entities.body: The Persian king named as an example of a lawgiver.

entities.name: Gorgias
entities.body: The celebrated Greek teacher of rhetoric, from Leontini.

entities.name: Thrasymachus
entities.body: The teacher of rhetoric from Chalcedon, also called the Chalcedonian giant.

entities.name: Theodorus of Byzantium
entities.body: The teacher of rhetoric whose elaborate divisions of a speech are discussed.

entities.name: Zeno of Elea
entities.body: The philosopher renowned for paradoxes, playfully called the Eleatic Palamedes.

entities.name: Evenus of Paros
entities.body: The poet and teacher of rhetoric credited with indirect praise and censure.

entities.name: Tisias
entities.body: The Sicilian teacher of rhetoric associated here with arguments from probability.

entities.name: Prodicus
entities.body: The sophist known for distinctions between words and their meanings.

entities.name: Hippias of Elis
entities.body: The sophist and teacher called the Elean stranger.

entities.name: Polus
entities.body: The teacher of rhetoric whose collection of technical terms is discussed.

entities.name: Licymnius
entities.body: The poet and teacher of rhetoric credited with supplying Polus’s terminology.

entities.name: Protagoras
entities.body: The sophist cited for rules of correct expression.

entities.name: Eryximachus
entities.body: The physician who is Phaedrus’s friend and Acumenus’s son.

entities.name: Sophocles
entities.body: The Athenian tragic playwright used as an example of mastery of a whole art.

entities.name: Euripides
entities.body: The Athenian tragic playwright named alongside Sophocles.

entities.name: Pericles
entities.body: The Athenian statesman and orator whose education Socrates praises.

entities.name: Anaxagoras
entities.body: The philosopher whose teaching about nature and mind influenced Pericles.

entities.name: Hippocrates
entities.body: The Greek physician whose approach to understanding the body is compared with rhetoric.

entities.name: Isocrates
entities.body: The orator whom Socrates names as a promising friend at the close of the dialogue.

entities.name: Cicero
entities.body: The Roman author cited in the translator’s note about the Tusculan Disputations.

entities.name: Zeus
entities.body: The chief Olympian god, who leads the divine procession in Socrates’ account of the soul.

entities.name: Boreas
entities.body: The Greek god of the north wind, linked with Orithyia in the local legend.

entities.name: Orithyia
entities.body: The Athenian princess carried away by Boreas in the legend discussed beside the stream.

entities.name: Artemis
entities.body: The Greek goddess whose nearby temple is mentioned.

entities.name: Pharmacia
entities.body: Orithyia’s companion in the version of the story Socrates considers.

entities.name: The centaurs
entities.body: The half-human, half-horse beings called Hippocentaurs in the discussion of myths.

entities.name: The chimeras
entities.body: The composite monsters mentioned among stories that resist rational explanation.

entities.name: The Gorgons
entities.body: The fearsome female monsters of Greek myth.

entities.name: Typhon
entities.body: The monstrous being called Typho, with whom Socrates compares his own unexplored nature.

entities.name: Hera
entities.body: The Olympian goddess and wife of Zeus, called Here in the original translation.

entities.name: Achelous
entities.body: The river god honored at the place where Socrates and Phaedrus rest.

entities.name: The Nymphs
entities.body: The nature divinities associated with the stream and the speakers’ inspiration.

entities.name: The Muses
entities.body: The goddesses of poetry, music and inspired learning.

entities.name: Eros
entities.body: The god of love, son of Aphrodite in the account discussed here.

entities.name: Aphrodite
entities.body: The Greek goddess of love and beauty.

entities.name: Helen
entities.body: Helen of Troy, the woman whom Stesichorus reviles and then praises in his recantation.

entities.name: The Sibyl
entities.body: The inspired prophetess cited as an example of divine madness.

entities.name: Hestia
entities.body: The goddess of the hearth, who remains at home in the divine procession.

entities.name: Ares
entities.body: The Greek god of war, whose followers Socrates describes.

entities.name: Apollo
entities.body: The Greek god associated with prophecy and inspiration.

entities.name: Ganymede
entities.body: The beautiful youth loved by Zeus in the myth recalled by Socrates.

entities.name: Odysseus
entities.body: The Homeric hero renowned for resourceful speech, used in comparisons with rhetoricians.

entities.name: Terpsichore
entities.body: The Muse associated here with dancers in the story of the cicadas.

entities.name: Erato
entities.body: The Muse associated here with lovers in the story of the cicadas.

entities.name: Calliope
entities.body: The eldest Muse, associated here with philosophy and elevated discourse.

entities.name: Urania
entities.body: The Muse associated with heaven and thought in Socrates’ account.

entities.name: Nestor
entities.body: The wise old king of Pylos in Homer, used as a model of eloquent speech.

entities.name: Palamedes
entities.body: The Greek hero famous for ingenuity, named in the comparison about rhetoric.

entities.name: Pan
entities.body: The rustic god invoked in Socrates’ closing prayer.

entities.name: Hermes
entities.body: The Greek messenger god invoked in the conversation.

entities.name: Midas
entities.body: The Phrygian king named in the quoted tomb inscription.

entities.name: Dionysus
entities.body: The Greek god associated with initiatory religious madness.

entities.name: Adrastus
entities.body: The legendary king of Argos praised for his honeyed eloquence.

entities.name: Theuth
entities.body: The Egyptian god, usually called Thoth, credited with inventing writing in Socrates’ story.

entities.name: Thamus
entities.body: The Egyptian king and god who judges Theuth’s inventions, identified here with Ammon.

entities.name: Adonis
entities.body: The mythological youth honored in the short-lived gardens used as Socrates’ comparison.

entities.name: God
entities.body: The divine nature or a divine patron invoked in Socrates’ account of souls.

entities.name: The Cypselids
entities.body: The ruling family of ancient Corinth, recalled for its lavish offerings at Olympia.

entities.name: The youth in Lysias’s speech
entities.body: The imagined young man addressed by the speaker in Lysias’s speech.

entities.name: The speaker in Lysias’s speech
entities.body: The imagined suitor who presents himself as a non-lover.

entities.name: The youth in Socrates’ speech
entities.body: The imagined young man addressed in Socrates’ speeches about love.

entities.name: The concealed lover
entities.body: The suitor in Socrates’ invented story who pretends not to love the youth.

entities.name: The Delphic priestess
entities.body: The prophetess of Apollo at Delphi, cited as an example of inspired speech.

entities.name: The priestesses of Dodona
entities.body: The women associated with the oracle at Dodona in the discussion of divine inspiration.

entities.name: The charioteer
entities.body: The driver in Socrates’ image of the soul, trying to guide its pair of winged horses.

entities.name: The noble horse
entities.body: The obedient horse in the image of the human soul, responsive to guidance and restraint.

entities.name: The unruly horse
entities.body: The resistant horse in the image of the human soul, pulling against the driver’s guidance.

entities.name: The cicadas
entities.body: The singing insects, called grasshoppers in the tale, whom Socrates connects with the Muses.

entities.name: The bronze maiden
entities.body: The speaking statue in the quoted inscription on Midas’s tomb.
